title: Consumer‐Mediated Nutrient Cycling in Marine Environments: A Global Meta‐Analysis
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

Animals release nutrients through their metabolic waste products, which can bolster primary productivity. For a given level of nutrient provisioning, we should expect the largest effect on primary producers to occur in more nutrient-limited waters, but empirical tests for global-scale patterns of animal-mediated provisioning effects on primary producers are lacking. Here, we quantify the magnitude and variability of the effect of provisioning across marine taxa and regions.

Location

Global.

Time Period

1900–2024.

Major Taxa Studied

Marine primary producers, invertebrates, fishes and birds.

Methods

Using a systematic review and meta-analysis, we collated 246 effect sizes drawn from 43 studies to quantify the growth benefit of nutrient provisioning by animals to various primary producers in experimental settings and along natural gradients. We compared the effect of provisioning on productivity for each major group of primary producers across latitudes, sea surface temperatures, levels of ambient nitrogen and phosphorus concentrations, levels of experimentally supplied nitrogen and considered several additional biological and experimental covariates.

Results

We found a variable but generally positive effect of provisioning on productivity. Macroalgae, corals and phytoplankton responded consistently positively to provisioning, but the responses of seagrass and endosymbionts were more variable. The response of macroalgae to provisioning was stronger in higher-latitude, cool, nitrogen-rich waters, even when controlling for the level of experimental nitrogen provisioning by animals. In contrast, the response of seagrass was stronger in warmer waters, and to a lesser extent, low latitudes. We found no global trends in the response of phytoplankton, corals, or endosymbionts and the level of nitrogen provisioning only increased the response of macroalgae and phytoplankton. Not enough studies reported phosphorus concentrations to properly investigate this potential moderator.

Main Conclusions

Our results suggest animal-provisioned nutrients enhance primary productivity across a broad range of ecological contexts. Contrary to our predictions, we found limited evidence that nutrient provisioning by animals had an overall stronger effect on primary producers in nitrogen-poor waters than in nitrogen-rich waters, but the differences between regions varied strongly among primary producer groups.
